name: Balance training
pattern: Standing on one leg or on an unstable surface and keeping your centre of mass over a small base of support.
setup: Stand next to a wall, counter or sturdy chair you can touch if you wobble.
Barefoot or flat shoes, feet hip width.
Eyes on a fixed point at eye level.

steps.text: Shift your weight onto one foot, spreading the toes.
Lift the other foot a few centimetres, knee soft on the standing leg.
Hold 20-40 seconds, making small corrections at the ankle; switch legs.

cues.cue: Grip the floor lightly: big toe, little toe and heel down.
cues.why: The small foot and lower-leg muscles make most of the fine corrections.
A slight bend lets the hip and knee help absorb wobbles.

cues.cue: Hips level; don't let the free side drop.
cues.why: The gluteus medius holds the pelvis level over one leg.

cues.cue: 20-40 s per hold, about 4 drills, 2 sets, 3 times a week.
cues.why: These were the most effective training doses for steady balance in young adults.

cues.cue: Make it harder one step at a time: eyes closed, soft pad, then board.
cues.why: Wobble boards and BOSU raise lower-limb muscle activity the most.

cues.cue: Keep it in your routine for good.
cues.why: Balance work prevents falls in older adults and repeat ankle sprains in active people.

breathing: Breathe slowly and normally; holding your breath makes you stiff.

tempo.note: Hold 20-40 s, rest, repeat 2 sets each leg.

mistakes.name: Hip drops or hikes
mistakes.looks: The pelvis tilts down on the free-leg side, or the body leans far over the standing foot.
mistakes.fix: Hips level, squeeze the standing-side glute.
mistakes.why: The hip abductors are not holding; you balance by leaning instead.

mistakes.name: Standing knee locked
mistakes.looks: The standing leg is snapped straight and rigid.
mistakes.why: Takes the hip and knee out of balance control.

mistakes.name: Arms flail or grab
mistakes.looks: Arms swing wide and the hand keeps grabbing the support.
mistakes.fix: Make it easier until you can hold 20 s, then progress.
mistakes.why: The drill is too hard to train the ankle strategy.

safety: Always have a wall or chair within reach; clear the floor around you.
Older adults: balance and functional exercise is the best-proven way to prevent falls, but start supported.
Recent ankle sprain: start on the floor, eyes open, when standing is pain-free.

variants.change: Soft surface: more ankle and calf work, larger wobbles.
Wobble board: highest muscle activity, hardest; start on two feet.
Stand on one leg and tap the other foot forward, side and back: reaching drill, like the Star Excursion test.
On one leg, rotate the pelvis open and closed over the standing hip.

harder: single leg on a wobble board

subtypes.name: Balance board (two feet)
subtypes.change: Both feet on a wobble board, knees soft; keep the board edges off the floor.

subtypes.name: Three-point toe tap
subtypes.change: Stand on the left leg in a quarter squat, tap the right toe forward, out to the side and behind, back to centre each time.

subtypes.name: Standing hip rotation
subtypes.change: On the left leg, knee lifted, turn the pelvis and trunk open to the right and back, foot fixed.

subtypes.name: Tightrope walk
subtypes.change: Walk heel-to-toe along a line, arms out, eyes ahead.

metrics.label: Hold on one leg
metrics.good: about 40 s eyes open, under 10 s eyes closed is typical for adults under 40; drops with age

motion.basis: Default: single-leg stance on the left leg. Joint angles are estimates of a relaxed single-leg stand; hold norms from springer2007, dosing from lesinski2015, device and muscle-activity cues from sanchez2022. trunkRot (+ toward the right) is an extra key not yet in the README convention.
